summary: What a probability "given" some information means, how to compute it, and when extra information changes nothing (independence). Tree diagrams and Bayes' rule put these together for problems in two stages.
objectives: Explain P(A | B) as a probability on the reduced sample space B
Use P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) and the multiplication rule
Build a tree diagram and read probabilities off it
Apply Bayes' rule to turn a conditional probability around

blocks.p: `P(A | B)` is the probability of A once you know that B happened. Knowing B throws away every outcome outside B, so B becomes the new sample space and only the part of A inside B still counts.
Example: roll one die and learn the result is even. The possible outcomes are now {2, 4, 6}, so P(6 | even) = 1/3, not the 1/6 you had before.

blocks.tip: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are different numbers in general. Read the bar as "given" and check which event is known.

sections.title: The formula and the multiplication rule

blocks.code:
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)        (P(B) > 0)
P(A ∩ B) = P(B) x P(A | B) = P(A) x P(B | A)

blocks.p: The first line is the definition. Multiply both sides by P(B) and you get the **multiplication rule**, which finds the probability that both events happen one step at a time.
Worked example: P(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4 give `P(A | B) = 0.12 / 0.4 = 0.3`.
A and B are **independent** when knowing one tells you nothing about the other. The test is:
Equivalently P(A | B) = P(A) when P(B) > 0. Two separate coin tosses are the standard example.

blocks.note: Disjoint and independent are different ideas. If A and B are disjoint and both have positive probability, they are **dependent**: learning B happened tells you A did not.

blocks.p: A tree splits an experiment into stages. Each branch carries a conditional probability; you **multiply along a path** to get a "both" probability and **add the paths** that make up the event you want.

figure.caption: A two-stage tree: P(A) = 0.3 x 0.9 + 0.7 x 0.2 = 0.41.

blocks.p: **Bayes' rule** turns a conditional probability around:

blocks.code: P(B | A) = P(A | B) x P(B) / P(A)

blocks.p: P(A) at the bottom usually comes from the tree: the sum of every path that ends in A.

blocks.tip: A positive result from a good test can still leave a low chance of having a rare condition. The small P(B) is why.

practice.q: P(A ∩ B) = 0.15 and P(B) = 0.5. Find P(A | B). If P(A) = 0.3, are A and B independent?

a.p: By the definition, P(A | B) = 0.15 / 0.5 = 0.3. This equals P(A), so knowing B does not change A: they are independent. The product test agrees: 0.3 x 0.5 = 0.15 = P(A ∩ B).

practice.q: A fair coin is tossed three times. Find the probability of three heads, and the probability of at least one tail.

a.p: Each toss is independent with P(H) = 1/2, so P(HHH) = 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8. "At least one tail" is the complement of HHH, so it is 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.

practice.q: A machine is faulty with probability 0.1. A faulty machine fails a check with probability 0.8; a working one fails with probability 0.05. A machine fails the check. Find the probability that it is faulty.

a.p: Let F = faulty and X = fails the check. P(X) = 0.8 x 0.1 + 0.05 x 0.9 = 0.08 + 0.045 = 0.125.

practice.q: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. Find P(A ∩ B) and P(A | B).

a.p: For independent events the intersection is the product: P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 x 0.5 = 0.15.
Then P(A | B) = 0.15 / 0.5 = 0.3, which is P(A), as independence says it must be.

a.note: The graded answer added the probabilities (0.8). Adding is the rule for disjoint events, not independent ones.

quiz.q: One die is rolled and the result is even. What is P(roll is 6 | even)?
quiz.explain: Given even, the outcomes are {2, 4, 6}, and 6 is one of three. 1/6 ignores the information.

quiz.q: P(A ∩ B) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.8. What is P(A | B)?
P(B) = 0.5 and P(A | B) = 0.6. What is P(A ∩ B)?
Which condition shows A and B are independent?
quiz.explain: The product test is the definition. An empty intersection means disjoint, which is a different idea.

quiz.q: In the tree on the slides (P(B) = 0.3, P(A | B) = 0.9, P(A | B') = 0.2), what is P(A)?
quiz.explain: Add both paths that end in A: 0.27 + 0.14 = 0.41.

quiz.q: Disjoint events with positive probabilities are independent.
quiz.explain: If one happens the other cannot, so knowing one changes the other: they are dependent.

quiz.q: P(A | B) is always equal to P(B | A).
quiz.explain: They differ in general; Bayes' rule is how you get from one to the other.

quiz.q: In the slides' test example, a positive result means about a 16% chance of having the condition.
quiz.explain: P(B | A) = 0.0095 / 0.059 = 0.161, small because the condition is rare.

cards.back: The probability of A when we know B happened.
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), with P(B) > 0
P(A ∩ B) = P(B) x P(A | B)
Disjoint: cannot happen together. Independent: one gives no information about the other. Disjoint events with positive probability are dependent.
Multiply along a path; add the paths that make up the event.
P(B | A) = P(A | B) x P(B) / P(A)

cards.front: Where P(A) in Bayes comes from
cards.back: The total of all tree paths ending in A, e.g. P(A | B)P(B) + P(A | B')P(B').
